wrong.text: Hold the thermometer in your palm to get a clearer view of the reading.

decisions.prompt: A student reads Six's thermometer. Which part of the index gives the correct reading?

options.text: The bottom of the index
options.consequence: That is the end the mercury pushed against, so the extreme is correct.

options.text: The top of the index
options.consequence: The reading is too far along by the length of the index, a common mistake.

options.text: The top of the mercury column
options.consequence: The mercury shows the present temperature, not the extreme.

decisions.prompt: The maximum and minimum have been written down. What should the observer do next with the thermometer?

options.text: Reset the indices with the magnet
options.consequence: The indices now start again from the present temperature for the next 24 hours.

options.text: Leave the indices as they are until next week
options.consequence: The next readings will be the old extremes and not the new day's.

options.text: Reset them by shaking the thermometer hard
options.consequence: Shaking can break the glass and disturb the mercury.

decisions.prompt: The wet-bulb muslin has dried out. What should be done before that reading is used?

options.text: Wet it with distilled water and wait for the bulb to settle
options.consequence: Evaporation returns, so the wet-bulb reading can be trusted.

options.text: Record it anyway, since the difference is small
options.consequence: A dry bulb reads like the dry-bulb thermometer, so humidity comes out far too high.

options.text: Wet it with tap water and read it straight away
options.consequence: Tap water leaves deposits, and the bulb has not had time to settle.

decisions.prompt: The school wants to move its Stevenson screen. Which site should be chosen?

options.text: In the open on short grass, away from buildings and trees
options.consequence: Air moves freely and readings are free from nearby heat and shade.

options.text: Next to the concrete wall of the staff room, for security
options.consequence: Heat from the wall affects the readings, a listed source of error.

options.text: Under a large mango tree, to keep it out of the sun
options.consequence: The shade changes the readings, which should represent open air.

observations.prompt: Four record sheets give the following dry-bulb and wet-bulb readings. Which one shows the highest relative humidity?

options.text: Dry 28 °C, wet 27 °C
Dry 30 °C, wet 26 °C
options.why: A depression of 4 °C means drier air.

options.text: Dry 32 °C, wet 24 °C
options.why: A depression of 8 °C means much drier air.

options.text: Dry 26 °C, wet 22 °C
options.why: A depression of 4 °C means drier air than a depression of 1 °C.

observations.prompt: A week's hourly record is examined. When do the extremes of temperature usually occur?

options.text: Maximum in early afternoon, minimum just before dawn
Maximum at noon exactly, minimum at midnight
options.why: The ground goes on heating after noon, and cooling continues until dawn.

options.text: Maximum at sunset, minimum at midday
options.why: Midday is warm, and the coolest time is just before dawn.

lines.text: She worked out the daily range as maximum plus minimum.

lines.text: She wrote that the screen is painted white to look clean.

lines.text: She took the readings at 9 a.m. each day.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for taking accurate readings at a weather station.
written.explainPrompt: Why does the wet bulb read lower than the dry bulb, and what does a small difference between them mean?
written.explainGuide: Water evaporating from the muslin cools the wet bulb, so it reads lower. In humid air there is little evaporation, so a small difference means high relative humidity.

correct: Keep to the marked path when you go out to the instruments after rain.

wrong.text: Climb the pole to read the wind vane more easily.
wrong.why: Do not climb on roofs or poles to read instruments.

wrong.text: Stay at the station to record the storm as it happens.
wrong.why: Avoid the station during thunderstorms.

wrong.why: Never climb on roofs. Read it from the ground.

wrong.text: Stop the anemometer cups with your fingers so that you can see them.
wrong.why: That risks injury and damages the instrument.

wrong.text: Run across the wet compound to get the reading on time.
wrong.why: Wet ground is slippery. Walk carefully.

options.text: In the open field, away from trees and buildings

options.text: Under the mango tree, where it will not be disturbed

options.text: Against a wall of the school building
options.consequence: Walls shelter the gauge and give splash-in during storms.

decisions.prompt: The vane's arrow points towards the north-east. What should be recorded?

options.text: A north-east wind
options.consequence: The arrow points to where the wind blows from, and winds are named that way.

options.text: A south-west wind
options.consequence: That confuses where the wind is going with where it comes from.

options.text: A north wind
options.consequence: The vane gives a more exact direction, so this is not accurate.

decisions.prompt: Dark clouds gather and thunder is heard at the usual time for readings. What should the observer do?

options.text: Wait indoors and take the readings when the storm has passed
options.consequence: The observer stays safe. The gauge keeps collecting the rain.

options.text: Run out to the station to finish before the rain
options.consequence: Thunderstorms are dangerous in the open, and the station must be avoided.

options.text: Shelter under the tall tree near the station until it stops
options.consequence: Tall trees attract lightning and are unsafe in a storm.

decisions.prompt: You need the monthly rainfall figure from the daily records. How do you get it?

options.text: Add up the daily totals
options.consequence: That gives the total rainfall for the month.

options.text: Add up the weekly means
options.consequence: Means are averages, so adding them does not give the total.

options.text: Take the largest daily figure
options.consequence: That is the wettest day only, and not the month's total.

observations.prompt: The measuring cylinder holds the collected rainwater. How should it be read?

options.text: At eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus
From above, at the top of the meniscus
options.why: That gives a parallax error and reads too high.

options.text: Held up high, at arm's length
options.why: Reading it above eye level gives a parallax error.

observations.prompt: A station's records for Nigeria show a change of wind with the seasons. Which pattern fits?

options.text: South-west in the wet season, north-east in the dry season
North-east in the wet season, south-west in the dry season
options.why: The harmattan from the north-east blows in the dry season.

options.text: Westerly throughout the year
options.why: The direction changes with the seasons.

observations.prompt: Which instrument gives the pressure in millibars?

options.text: Barometer
Hygrometer
options.why: A hygrometer measures humidity.

options.text: Anemometer
options.why: An anemometer measures wind speed.

options.text: Wind vane
options.why: A wind vane shows wind direction.

numerics.prompt: Rainfall for a week was 0, 12, 25, 0, 8, 30 and 5 mm. What is the total for the week?
Rainfall for a week was 0, 12, 25, 0, 8, 30 and 5 mm. What is the mean rainfall per day?
numerics.working: Total = 80 mm. Mean = 80 / 7 = {answer} mm per day.

numerics.prompt: Rainfall on four days was {a}, {b}, {c} and {d} mm. What is the total?
Anemometer cups on a circle of radius {r} m make {n} revolutions per minute. Taking circumference x revolutions / 60, what is the approximate wind speed, in m/s?
numerics.working: Circumference = 2 x pi x {r}. Speed = circumference x {n} / 60 = {answer} m/s.

written.explainPrompt: Why should a rain gauge be sited away from trees and buildings?
written.explainGuide: Trees and buildings shelter the gauge from rain and let water drip or splash into it. In open ground the funnel catches only the rain that falls, so the reading is accurate.

wrong.why: Rinse spills with water and do not touch them.

wrong.text: Pour leftover acid back into the main bottle to avoid waste.

decisions.prompt: Your granite sample is brown and crumbly on the outside. How should it be examined?

options.text: Look at a fresh surface, away from the weathered part
options.consequence: Weathering hides features, so a fresh surface shows the true crystals.

options.text: Describe the brown outside, as that is what you see
options.consequence: The weathered surface does not show the rock's true features.

options.text: Soak the sample in acid to clean the surface
options.consequence: Acid is used only as a drop test, and this would waste it and be unsafe.

decisions.prompt: A sample has fizzed and the test is over. What must be done before anything else is done with it?

options.text: Rinse the rock with water
options.consequence: No acid is left on the rock, so it is safe to handle and to test again.

options.text: Put it straight on the balance

options.text: Dry it on your uniform
options.consequence: That puts acid on your clothing and skin.

decisions.prompt: When the rock is lowered into the cylinder, bubbles cling to its surface. What should be done?

options.text: Gently move the thread to free the bubbles, then read

options.text: Read the level straight away, as they are small

options.consequence: That changes the starting level, so the volume is wrong.

decisions.prompt: A sample labelled gneiss shows clear bands of light and dark minerals. How is it classified?

options.text: Metamorphic
options.consequence: Banding in gneiss comes from heat and pressure.

options.text: Sedimentary, because it has layers

options.text: Igneous, because it is hard
options.consequence: Hardness alone does not show how a rock was formed.

observations.prompt: Which pair of samples should both fizz with the dilute acid?

options.text: Limestone and marble
Granite and basalt

options.text: Quartzite and sandstone

options.text: Shale and granite

options.text: Coarse, interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica
Dark and fine-grained

options.text: Fine layers that split easily
options.why: That describes shale.

options.text: Gritty grains cemented together

written.explainPrompt: Why do limestone and marble fizz when dilute acid is added, while quartzite does not?
written.explainGuide: Limestone and marble contain calcium carbonate, which reacts with the acid to release carbon dioxide gas. Quartzite is mainly quartz, which does not react.

decisions.prompt: At a monthly visit one pin has been knocked sideways by a goat. What should be done with its reading?

options.text: Note it and leave that pin out of the mean
options.consequence: The disturbed pin is a known source of error and is not treated as soil loss.

options.text: Use it just like all the others
options.consequence: A knocked pin does not show soil loss, so the mean is misleading.

options.text: Replace all the pins and begin again
options.consequence: Months of good data would be lost because of one pin.

numerics.working: Depth = {c} / 100 m. Volume = {s} x {s} x depth = {answer} m³.

faults.scenario: Adamu's erosion study was marked down for its method. Here is what he did and wrote.

lines.text: He studied only a bare plot, with no vegetated plot.
lines.why: A vegetated plot is needed as a control.

lines.text: He used plots of different sizes on different slopes.
lines.why: Plots need equal sizes and similar slopes for a fair test.

lines.text: He explained his results without mentioning rainfall.
lines.why: Results must be linked to rainfall.

lines.text: He hammered his pins in vertically to the same height.
lines.why: That is correct.

lines.text: He took readings at the same intervals.
lines.why: That lets him compare the months.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions when using erosion pins to measure soil loss.
written.explainPrompt: Why are the erosion pins on a bare plot usually more exposed than those on a grassed plot?
written.explainGuide: Bare soil has no cover, so raindrops and runoff remove it easily. Grass protects the surface and its roots hold the soil, slowing the runoff and reducing soil loss.
